utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, I asked that the witness be kept out so that we could discuss the administrative matters, the timings of the hearings this week and, indeed, the next sitting week. Beginning with today, how much longer are you likely to be? We are at paragraph -- you can remind me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 36, yes. So you're more than halfway through the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Most definitely, Mr. President, and the Court will no doubt notice that he's touched on some of the issues that are contained in the rest of the outline, so I would hope that I would be through with this witness in under an hour and perhaps 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then for the rest of the week, we've just been given the summary of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The next witness is testifying in open session. Mr. Naumovski will handle him. I would anticipate no more than an hour and a half to two hours in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's here, is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. And then we have one more witness, Mr. President, coming in tomorrow for Friday, and I've communicated to the senior legal officer he has scheduling difficulties that require him to finish up his testimony on Friday. So we will try to make sure that we do not take more than an hour and a half with him on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, because I don't know the position about Judge Bennouna, as to whether he's going to be available on Friday or not. It may be convenient to deal with now, while it's in our minds, with tomorrow's hearing. Is there any objection to Judge Robinson and I sitting tomorrow and Friday alone, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, speaking on behalf of Mr. Nice, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll make an order to that effect, covering Thursday and, if necessary, Friday. It's not the practice -- it hasn't been the practice to sit on Friday afternoon. You're anticipating getting through in an hour and a half, yes, so it may be necessary to sit in the afternoon, but not extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would think that's accurate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, considering the position today and tomorrow, I have to take a longer-than-usual lunch break, so we'll have to adjourn at half past 12.00 tomorrow until half past 2.00. This witness, Mr. Vucina, is ready to give evidence this afternoon, if necessary; would that be the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But could give evidence and presumably could be through tomorrow comfortably?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I cannot imagine that he will not be complete by the end of the day tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This afternoon is supposed to be a Chambers day. There are other matters which we've got to deal with. The other matter is that there's going to be a scheduling conference -- a status conference in another case, which will involve, of course, the court staff beginning at half past 4.00, and also the interpreters, and it's apparently anticipated to go on for quite some time; it may be until 6.00. So it may be fair to give everybody else besides us a break during the afternoon. So would it be convenient to deal with this witness -- finish this witness today and deal with the other witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's completely acceptable from our side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and we would finish tomorrow morning, probably, or early afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, that being the position, does it seem a practical way of going along, dealing with one witness today? How long do you anticipate you'll be in cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will certainly endeavour to finish everything up today, so I think it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I appreciate the Court's situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Quite honestly, the earlier the better, so that we can give the court staff a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As we made Your Honour aware yesterday, we were taken a bit by surprise by the nature of the testimony of this witness, so we're trying to act accordingly and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you slow down, please. Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we'll hear this witness today, the next witness tomorrow, and the final witness on Friday. If necessary, we'll sit into the afternoon. We should also deal with the -- there's an outstanding argument about the affidavits which has got to be resolved, as I understand it, last week's affidavits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If there are any objections to the affidavits, then those objections should probably be resolved on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Somers, will you be ready to deal with those affidavits on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will speak with Mr. Nice and see which -- I'm confident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Maric affidavits. There are about five which are outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I get back to the Court after the break, and I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, here he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry not to be here when administrative matters were being dealt with. I was catching up with progress elsewhere. Affidavits for last week, yes, we should be able to deal with those, of course, on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But it had occurred to me that I should tell you that our intention is to raise another argument which could conveniently be dealt with this week. It relates to one of the Defence experts, the military expert. He is scheduled to come here the week after next. Now, we're going to apply to exclude his evidence altogether on the grounds that it doesn't qualify as expert in accordance with this Chamber's earlier rulings. There's a short written brief that's been prepared which will be filed almost immediately, and although we've been subject to minimum periods in relation to the witness, we wouldn't want to inconvenience the witness himself. The problem with leaving the argument until the week after next is that he will already have flown here from America and will be personally inconvenienced if the argument succeeds and his evidence is excluded. So we thought that it might be helpful to raise that argument this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well let us have the brief as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a very extensive report, it's 100 pages of report and I'm not suggesting the Chamber would be in any position to read it in detail, but it might be able to skim it so as to understand the points that we are going to be making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is which -- what's the name of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His name is Schrader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Schrader, very well. We'll look at that in due course. I'm not sure that we have had the testimony yet but we may have done. We have, yes. Very well, we'll have that in mind. And while I am dealing with administrative matters and that week, we shall not be sitting in this case on Friday the 23rd. There are other matters before the Trial Chamber which we've got to hear that day but as a result, we are minded if necessary to sit later on the days of the week when we are sitting, that's the Tuesday until the Thursday, if necessary, until half past five in order to get through the work. Yes, now unless there are any other matters, we will then go on with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, I'm sorry you've been delayed but there were some administrative matters we had to deal with. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, we had reached that part of your outline that deals with the organisation of the military justice system. And you say in your outline, that a special effort was put into creating and organising military judicial bodies in the HZ HB. With whom did the primary responsibility for military justice lay?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary responsibility for military justice lay with the military command or ultimately the supreme commander of the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna. On the basis of regulations, that was the president of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the president of the HZ HB was Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Throughout its existence.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the existence of this institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, what military power, please tell the Court, what military power the vice-presidents of the Presidency had, if any?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the vice-presidents of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry if that was unclear. Let's take it one step at a time. With respect to the HZ HB, the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, what military authority did the vice-presidents of the Presidency Mr. Rajic and Mr. Kordic have?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the regulations of Herceg-Bosna, no mention has been made of special powers that vice-presidents of the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna have. The only thing that is stipulated is that the Presidency has two vice-presidents. That is to say, that is as far as powers are concerned or the authority of the vice-presidents of Herceg-Bosna, then these were actually powers exercised by the bodies as a whole not of individual members of that body, that is to say, of the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna. In this specific case, there were no special powers involved for the vice-president. However, with your permission, I would like to add one more sentence. The Presidency of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna practically lost all its authority towards the end of 1992. In fact, and legally it was not extinguished altogether but, in fact, it stopped to exist; it did not pass any decisions or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Staying on the subject of the authority of the Presidency and specifically the authority of vice-presidents of the Presidency in relation to military matters, what authority did the vice-presidents of the Presidency have with respect to the administration of the military justice system in the HZ HB, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one looks at the regulations of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, in the military domain that is, one may easily see that military prerogatives were enjoyed by the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. So it was not the Presidency as an institution, and not any of the vice-presidents either within that institution because it says there expressly that the supreme commander is the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, not the Presidency, that is, but the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did members of the Presidency individually have the power to appoint, remove or to discipline members of the armed forces, Mr. Perkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, because that would have been in contravention of the existing regulations for the highest commanders. It was within the domain of the powers of the president of Herceg-Bosna as the supreme commander. High officers had the responsibility to appoint lower-ranking officers within military formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning to paragraph 38, Your Honours, I believe the witness has already dealt with this so in a summary fashion let me just lead him through this. Mr. Perkovic, it's correct, is it not, that in the HZ HB and in the HR HB, trial and appellate courts were set up as constituting the military justice system and that these courts confirmed the applicability of the criminal statutes of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and preserved and provided for a right of appeal.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Both civilian and military courts confirmed the applicability and did indeed apply the criminal law, rather, the criminal code of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Criminal Code of the SFRY which was taken over by Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe you testified yesterday that there were four district military courts set up under the HZ HB and that they continued under the HR HB. These were, I believe, in Mostar, Livno, Bosanski Brod and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since Bosanski Brod was under the control of Bosnian Serbs, the seat of this court was, in fact, in Orasje, but it was the basic military court for that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe that these district military courts had exclusive jurisdiction over war crimes committed by members of the military.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military courts had the jurisdiction to try members of the military who allegedly committed war crimes and also civilian persons who were in military service and who had allegedly committed war crimes. Also, crimes that could possibly have been committed by prisoners of war related to violations of humanitarian law, and crimes that pertained to violations of the humanitarian law, that is to say, the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe it's accurate to say that the Travnik District Military Court had jurisdiction in the Lasva Valley and other areas of Central Bosnia over the sorts of offences that you've just enumerated.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Its local jurisdiction was identical, I think, to the area of the military zone of Central Bosnia. I believe it was compatible with that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Perkovic, I think you've touched on several of the subjects from paragraph 39, 40 and 41, so let's try to address these issues in a fairly summary fashion. Could you just describe for the Court, to the extent that you have not already, what offences -- over which the district military courts exercised or exerted jurisdiction, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I'm speaking about this, these are, in principle, all criminal offences in view of the persons who committed them. However, if we are to specify these criminal offences, these are criminal offences inter alia belonging to the group of offences that are called criminal offences against humanity and humanitarian law. Within that category, there are other descriptions for a series of crimes against civilian populations, prisoners of war, et cetera; also the crime of genocide, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just looking over paragraph 39, Mr. Perkovic, I do believe that you've already provided your evidence on that, so there's no need to dwell on it. Just a matter of detail with respect to paragraph 40. Could you describe for the Court, please, the function of the district military prosecutor and also describe for the Court how many district military prosecutors' offices were set up in the HZ HB and continued on under the HR HB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I'm going to answer your second question. The number of the military district prosecutors was compatible to the number of military district courts, because in our practice the organisation of prosecutors' offices corresponded to that of the organisation of military courts. And now the other question. District military prosecutors had a subordinating role, if I may put it that way. That means that sometimes, when other relevant institutions within the military justice system did not want to institute criminal proceedings or could not, the district military prosecutor could take this over on the basis of the law, on the basis of regulations. He could institute criminal proceedings against perpetrators of certain crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And just proceeding on, could you just describe for the Court the circumstances under which appeals could be taken from district military court judgements, sir, and how those appeals were handled?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle. Well, there was the principle which made it possible to appeal. This was one of the basic principles upon which military and civilian justice was based. When rulings were passed by first-instance courts, both the prosecutor and the defence could lodge an appeal if they believed, of course, that such a ruling was unfair to either one side or the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I take it that trials before the district military courts were tried in public, not behind closed doors.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do not know of a single case of a trial behind closed doors, without the presence of the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, in cases involving sentences of up to five years, which courts handled such appeals?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as sentences of up to five years of imprisonment are concerned, in the appeals procedure it is a higher court that decided on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And what would be the situation if the sentence were to exceed five years; which tribunal would hear an appeal of a sentence of that magnitude?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since sentences exceeding five years were considered to correspond to graver crimes, it was the Supreme Court or, rather, a specific department of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina that handled these.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. With respect to paragraph 42, Your Honours, I believe the witness has already testified about that. There's no need to go into it. I just call your attention to Exhibit D276/1, tab 1, which was identified yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the independence of the judiciary and the justice system, Mr. Perkovic, just a few questions. Was the judiciary of the HZ HB and the HR HB, or the judicial bodies that were set up by those two institutions, independent from the legislative and executive branches or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning when the war broke out, there was -- for a very short while, there was some hesitation regarding the military judiciary, because the organisation of the military judiciary is regulated by decree rather than a decision of some executive body. And at a later stage, a special body was set up made of legal experts, that is, judges, representatives of courts, prosecutors, attorneys, lawyers, and they were responsible for the personnel policy in the judiciary. That was the only body authorised to nominate or designate judges, prosecutors and so on. No political institution did that. So in that sense, I can say that both the prosecutors' office and the judiciary in Herceg-Bosna were independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In connection with prosecutions initiated in the district military courts, who had the ability to initiate such a prosecution? Could you tell us that, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in relation to the military prosecution, proceedings could be launched at the request -- upon the motion of a military prosecutor filed with the relevant court or, say, District Military Court. Then the relevant judge in the relevant court -- that is, the Military Court conducted the relevant investigation, and after the conduct of these investigations, if there was suspicion that a crime had been committed, then the military prosecutor could file the charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The military judicial system, sir, was this part of, or completely independent from the military organisation of the armed forces themselves?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was basically independent of the armed forces. It was, conditionally speaking, a type of special courts, as they were defined in our legal practice. It was a part of a tradition in the former Yugoslavia, that is, they heard a specific type of crimes, crimes committed by military persons or persons in the military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, with either the public prosecutor's office or the district military prosecutor's office and prosecutions handled by both of those institutions, sir, was there any right on the part of a legislator or member of the legislative or the executive branch of government to interfere in any way with those processes as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individual procedures and individual cases, no. Of course, the executive power could change regulations governing the work of those courts, and it could also adopt a regulation to abolish those courts. But in individual cases, the legislative power and the executive branch of power did not interfere with the proceedings before these or the civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Perkovic. Let me turn to one subject, and I would like to discuss this only very briefly. You've previously provided testimony regarding the collapse of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina state institutions in the area of banking, insurance, the monetary system and so forth. What did you and your colleagues in the HZ HB do to try to provide for the normal functioning of economic life in your communities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the initial stage, when the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna began to adopt its own regulations, the majority of those regulations bore upon the economic sphere, business. So that regulations were adopted to regulate the founding and the operation of banks, insurance companies, regulations on public enterprises and so on and so forth. Why? Because the objective was to, as quickly as possible, create the legal prerequisites for the functioning of the civil, that is economic life in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina have a national bank?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What contacts, if any, did the institutions of the HZ HB or the HR HB have with this national bank, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All republics of the former Yugoslavia had their own national banks. But those national banks in contrast with the National Bank of Yugoslavia was not the bank of issue. Even though that was its name,"The National Bank","The National Banks". When the war began in Bosnia-Herzegovina, relevant contacts with representatives of financial institutions were maintained so that in August 1992, at Siroki Brijeg, that is in the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna directly, the prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Jure Pelivan and the minister of finance of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Mustafa or Mahmut Logo, I'm not sure, came to Siroki Brijeg. At that meeting, held then at Siroki Brijeg, the discussion also broached the subject of the issue of Bosnian legal tender, and those gentlemen showed a specimen of what that future currency of Bosnia-Herzegovina should look like. I do not know why or what reason these activities they told us about, about the preparation of this new currency coming to a halt, but I do know that even in Sarajevo, as the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina, until 1994, the new currency of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not in use. Instead, there was -- there were coupons which could be used to pay for some small things, small purchases such as newspapers or bread, say, and all the more substantive transactions were paid in German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that the HZ HB department of finance founded a public accounting office, the SDK and the SDK recognised that Croatian dinars could be paid in payment of debts. Why was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one reads more attentively the regulations of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna then one can see that in the early regulations, for instance, the chapter on fines, is in dinars. The dinar was the currency that is referred to. But when the war began in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the payments in Bosnia-Herzegovina came to a stop. Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have its own currency and, at the initial stage, the population began to use the German mark internally at first as the chief legal tender in any commodity transaction. When in Herceg-Bosna we decided to invest efforts into making the payments function again, which, of course, meant that all sorts of dues and taxes would have to be paid, taxes, contributions, donations and so on and so forth, we then had to face up to the problem as to what currency should we adopt. And in addition to the German mark, we opted for the Croatian dinar for the simple reason that over 90 per cent of the overall trade at that time was with the Republic of Croatia, because all the basic necessities of the population such as the purchase of foodstuffs and other items were purchased in the Republic of Croatia, from Croatia, because our enterprises at that time by and large did not work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much for that explanation, Mr. Perkovic. I think that clears that issue up. Now, let me just draw your attention to one of the decrees that was passed by the HZ HB, the decree on the registration of foreign enterprises. How were enterprises from the Republic of Croatia treated? Were they treated as domestic enterprises or were they treated as foreign enterprises?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All enterprises with the seat outside Bosnia-Herzegovina and all enterprises with their seat in the territory which we considered occupied by the Serbs who wanted to continue their activities and work in the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna had to be re-registered. That is, they had to go through the procedure of registration all over again. There was no automatic procedure, so all foreign enterprises had to go through the same procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no protection measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one further question on the issue of citizenship. We already covered that yesterday, but we've already seen as Exhibit D182/1 in this case there was a decree on enforcing the law of misdemeanours and in Article 7 dealing with the appointments of judges. The provision exists that a person who meets the conditions set out in Article 303 of the law on misdemeanours and who is a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina may be appointed a judge of the chamber, and this is a decree that was passed on the July 3, 1992. I take it, sir, that the -- or you tell us. Was ever a decree adopted that provided for the conferring of Croatian citizenship upon people within the HZ HB or did you ever have that power or authority?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will take the liberty of answering -- responding to your first statement. Not only the decree on misdemeanours, but all the other decrees as well required the citizenship of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a pre-condition. The decree on the armed forces says that a member of the Croat Defense Council may only be a national of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And a similar case applies to judges and many other important functions in all three branches of power, the legislative executive and judicial. Could you please remind me of the question that you asked me, the last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, the question was inelegantly phrased but let me just ask you this: Did you and your colleagues in the organs of government of first the HZ HB and within the HVO subsequently in the HR HB, did you consider yourselves to be citizens of the Republic of Croatia or of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croat Community and the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna to begin with never adopted a regulation on the nationality of Herceg-Bosna. Throughout the war and before the war, the citizens in that territory were the nationals of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that is proven very easily by the fact that throughout the war, those citizens could request and get their nationality certificates where it was stated very explicitly. In other words, insofar as the nationality is concerned, we did not pass any laws unlike the other two, nor did we change anything. We could not change anything because we did not adopt anything like the other two parties, the Bosniak and the Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My next question concerns the question of language, sir, and I wonder if the usher could get a copy of Exhibit D276/1, the package of exhibits for you, and my question concerns tab 4. Tab 4, Mr. Perkovic, is a decree on the application of the law of government in the territory of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna in times of war or immediate threat of war, signed by the president of the HVO, Dr. Jadranko Prlic, on the 18th of February, 1993. Now, specifically, article 2 provides that the Croatian standard language and Latin script shall be officially used by government bodies of the HZ HB, but it also states that residents of the HZ HB shall have the right to use their own language and script in communication with government bodies of the HZ HB. Was any regulation, decree, or decision passed, as far as you're aware, that prohibited anybody from using the language that hitherto they had used within the municipalities encompassed by the HZ HB or the HR HB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no such regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me go on to the next subject, sir, which concerns the question of the constitutionality of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. In the days surrounding the foundation of the HZ HB on the 18th of November, 1991, were you asked to undertake any analysis of the constitutionality of the organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three days following the establishment of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna, my colleague and I were called by a Croat minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he asked us to prepare our opinion in writing for the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was Mr. Miro Lasic. And that opinion, that is, how he explained it to us, was to serve as a foundation for the request to be submitted by the government to the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina to proclaim the Croat -- to proclaim anti-constitutional the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna, so that we were placed in charge of that. And so we spent two or three days working on that. We wrote our opinion down and informed the minister, that is, Mr. Lasic. I also notified my minister of justice, Mr. Nikolic, that there was no constitutional foundation for the annulment -- for the abolition of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna because the preamble of the decision on its foundation figures the HDZ, that is, as a party founding that community. And the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, which was the end of November of 1991, considered this opinion and decided that there were no grounds to file the charges -- to file the case with the Constitutional Court and, therefore, never launched the procedure before the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now you're discussing the actions or the decisions not to act taken by the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 1991, early-1992 time frame.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, the constitution that existed at that time, I gather, was the 1974 version of the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And until the foundation of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, following the signature of the Washington Agreement and the Dayton Agreements, did the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after its foundation or declaration of its existence on the 6th of March, 1992, did it ever adopt its own constitution?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitution of 1974 -- the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina of 1974, until the Dayton -- that is, the Washington Accords, was not basically changed. Relevant amendments to that constitution did take place, but it was still under socialism before the multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina and those amendments were irrelevant, were immaterial. They were more of a cosmetic nature. But when these parties won the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, until as late as the end of the war, that is, the Washington and Dayton Accords, this constitution was not changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Perkovic, I don't want to ask you any opinions that you have or may have concerning the Constitutional Court decision dated September [realtime transcript read in error "December"] the 14th, 1992, but I will ask you this: You were in the justice department of the HZ HB at that time. Was any notice provided to your department of the pendency of proceedings before the Constitutional Court to declare or to consider the constitutionality of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I personally did not know, but I think that in the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna, not only the Minister of Justice or, rather, the Department of Justice, as it was called then and in all other institutions, nobody had any idea that the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina was deliberating the constitutionality of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, we can't go on for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if we're working and we're on air. Mr. Sayers, are you hearing us?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I can hear you now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've just lost the witness, who has had to take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might, Mr. President, let me take this opportunity to correct one error on the transcript at line 23 and 24 on page 27. The date of the Constitutional Court decision under consideration is 14 September, not December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers. The matter that you were dealing with is whether the witness, in his department, had notice of the proceedings before the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I wonder -- Mr. Perkovic, there was a technical problem. I wonder if you could just repeat the testimony that you just gave for the Court.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I stated ultimately -- I don't know when the Honourable Judges stopped receiving the interpretation. But Bosnia and Herzegovina assessed that there was no need to initiate proceedings to establish the constitutionality of the establishment of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. You asked me --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The point where the technical problem occurred was where we were asking you whether you, in the justice department or any body of the HZ HB, as far as you're aware, received notice of the pendency of proceedings before the Constitutional Court before it issued its decision on the 14th of September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one, no one in the justice department. And I personally think that no one else in government bodies of Herceg-Bosna realised there were proceedings going on to establish the constitutionality of Herceg-Bosna, nor were they officially made aware of the ruling that was passed ultimately by the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was any opportunity to appear before the court to participant in these proceedings ever afforded to the justice department of the HZ HB or to the HZ HB generally?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there were such opportunities because the representatives of the authorities from Sarajevo at that time came to this area very often for various meetings. Various meetings related to the procurement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to participate in the consideration of this particular decision that was issued by the Constitutional Court on the 14th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because neither I nor anyone else, I think, did not even know about it until it was actually decided upon. So, we had no opportunity. But there was an opportunity for them to inform us the proceedings were under way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a different point and one that was appropriately made. Now, did you ever receive a copy of the decision of the Constitutional Court, anyone in the justice department or anyone in the HZ HB, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not. I personally first saw this decision in 1995 when I came to Sarajevo for the first or second time and when I was personally interested in seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, one of the witnesses in this case, Professor Ribicic, has asserted that the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of Justice recommended to the government that it should bring an action against the HZ HB before the Constitutional Court on the grounds that the HZ HB was assertedly unconstitutional. Now you were in the Ministry of Justice at that time, sir. Is that contention factually accurate or is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No that is not correct. On the contrary, I said a few minutes ago that the Ministry of Justice gave a completely contrary opinion to that presented by Mr. Ribicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Perkovic, we're on the home straight now. Let me just tell you that one of the positions advanced by the Prosecution in this case is that the political institutions of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were designed to foster a system of widespread and systematic persecution of and discrimination against Bosnian Muslims. You, yourself, participated in the drafting of a large quantity of these decrees and decisions, sir. Is there anything in the position advanced by the Prosecution as I have related it to you? Could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my personal profound conviction, in all the regulations of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and later the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna as well, there are no discriminatory regulations vis-a-vis any category of population on any grounds including ethnic. That is to say, I am convinced that the legal system of Herceg-Bosna both the Community and the Republic did not have any discriminatory legislation of one social group at the expense of another group, specifically, the Croats at the expense of others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I apologise to have to interrupt but I believe this is exactly the kind of objection that we lodged yesterday, that this is an opinion that this man is simply not qualified to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I disagree. We, as a Trial Chamber, ruled that the witness could give evidence about what he did and what he knew. If he was responsible for this legislation he is entitled to say that it wasn't discriminatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, along the lines of the testimony that you were just giving, were you ever instructed by the superiors in the government or was it ever suggested to you, in a subtle or indirect way rather than directly, or maybe too that the laws should be slanted in favour of the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the territory of the HZ HB as opposed to another ethnic group such as Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Let me move on to the last subject or the last set of subjects. Have you ever heard Mr. Kordic ever say derogatory or pejorative things about any ethnic groups other than the one to which he belongs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of Mr. Kordic ever having any military functions as opposed to political functions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for hierarchy and military subordination as established by the regulations of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Kordic was not part of that hierarchy. That is to say, that he, according to these regulations, did not have an appropriate military position within that hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've described Mr. Boban as the supreme commander, and we know from the two decrees on the armed forces that that's exactly what he was. Could you give the Court some feel for the personality of this man, because we haven't really had a lot of testimony about that, Mr. Perkovic, and I wonder if you could throw some light on that subject for us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Mate Boban was a person of uncontested authority and the leader of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that he was the only leader of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that context, his decisions were practically never questioned. When, in 1993, we prepared the decision on constituting the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, we envisaged then to adopt a special chapter within that decision that would deal with the institution of the president of the republic. We would try, therefore, to set appropriate limits on the way in which responsibility would be exercised in performing the duties of president of the republic. However, you saw that in that decision on the establishment of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna there is no such chapter, because practically we who were preparing that decision were not allowed to do that now. We were told, "Let it be. The time is not right for that now. Let go of that." We could not prepare anything like that because we simply did not have the power to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, was Mr. Kordic a member of the inner circle of decision makers in either the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna or the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the most important or fateful decisions for the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were, in essence, passed by the president of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Boban. I shall just remind you that it was Mr. Boban who signed all three peace plans; the Vance-Owen Plan, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, and the Cutilliero plan before these two plans. I know that as far as these plans were concerned, which were such crucial importance for us, appropriate bodies of Herceg-Bosna discussed them but only after they were signed. So these and other very important decisions were passed by Mr. Boban without previously discussing them in appropriate institutions of Herceg-Bosna. These deliberations took place later, after these plans were actually signed. In this way, I'm trying to tell you that Mr. Boban, indeed, had uncontested authority and had -- how should I put this -- supreme power in making all decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the question, sir, of what powers were exercised by a vice-president of the Presidency of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. We have already seen, and it's in evidence as Exhibit D181/1 at Tab 3 that there is a code of practice that was adopted on the 17th of October of 1992 dealing with the work of the Presidency of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. Could you tell us, sir, what the powers of a vice-president of the Presidency -- what the powers of the two vice-presidents of the Presidency were?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vice-president, on the basis of these rules of procedure, has the duty to help the president in carrying out these tasks. That is to say, to help prepare sessions of the Presidency to carry out those duties that the president would transfer upon them in order to take away some of his own load and also to chair meetings of the Presidency when the president is absent. That is to say, that according to these rules of procedure and other regulations, the vice-presidents of Herceg-Bosna did not have any functions of their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just turn to the period of time between the foundation of the HR HB on the 28th of August, 1993 to February 17th of 1994. Did Mr. Kordic hold any position of significance within the government of the HR HB during those periods of time, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I know that at that time, Mr. Kordic did not hold any significant position, partly due to the fact that throughout this period that you are referring to, Mr. Kordic was not in the area where these institutions of government of Herceg-Bosna were functioning. I think that he was cut off all the time in this Lasva Valley without the possibility of having physical contact with the rest of, the area down there, of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The Prosecution in this case has tried to contend that all of the political institutions of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1991 and the signature of the Washington Agreement in the spring of 1994 systematically excluded Muslims from all positions of power. Could you just turn to Tab 5 of your exhibit booklet, Mr. Perkovic. This is a compilation of the Muslims who were in the positions of government in both institutions. Could you tell the Court whether there was, indeed, any policy to exclude systematically Muslims from positions of power or authority within the governmental institutions of the HZ HB or HR HB.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such policy. This is supported by a certain fact. In addition to the names of these persons, I wish to state that during the first stage of the war, a large number of HVO members were of Bosniak Muslim ethnicity. That even the commander of the operations for the liberation of Mostar, that is to say the commander of the HVO, was a Muslim, Mr. Amir Jaganjac. That the deputy minister of the interior of Herceg-Bosna at the time was a Bosniak Muslim as well. That an enormous or relatively big number of Bosniaks worked in municipal administrations within Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just two final subjects, sir. We have assembled a series of charts as Tab 6 of your exhibit booklet which just basically track the organisational structure of the government of Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna through its relevant time periods and the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Could you just confirm that these charts accurately represent the way the government was organised, and I'll just leave it open to the Prosecution to ask you questions about them, should they wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think these are accurate, but I cannot state very precisely right now that it was from such a date to such a date. For example, in the first table, you say the 18th of November, 1991, the 18th of April, 1992, and I cannot state exactly that those were the dates concerned but the schematics concerned are correct. The same goes for the other diagrams that you put into this chapter 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, well the dates we can derive from the documents, Mr. Perkovic. But generally speaking, do these diagrams accurately depict the evolution of the institutions of the HZ HB and HR HB over --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- 1991 to 1994. Thank you. And the final question, sir --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution contends in this case that, as I said, that there was a policy of widespread and systematic persecution against Muslims. During all the time that you worked in the HZ HB and HR HB did you ever see any indication that any people in the top decision-making groups had any intention, plan or policy of discriminating against or persecuting people of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna did not have a plan of ethnic persecution of the population on ethnic grounds, in this particular case of Muslim -- of Bosniaks. This community, this republic, did not have any such plans; nor did any of its institutions have such plans. I shall illustrate this by saying that in some parts of Herceg-Bosna, for example, Livno, the municipality of Livno, Tomislavgrad, Orasje, Posusje, Siroki Brijeg, Grude, et cetera, there was no such thing. I'm not precluding the possibility of perhaps such actions having been taken in certain very local environments that were aimed at intimidating the population or part of the population on ethnic grounds; but that was not the general policy. Nor was there a general plan of this kind within the institutions of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I do not have any other questions for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as Mr. Sayers covered all my interests, we have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, half past 11.00. We'll adjourn now until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, what is your actual current occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a lawyer by profession, and all my career was -- had to do with law. So I am now the head of the Office of the Vice-President of the Federation in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted clarified. Thank you. So you're currently working in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last five years I've spent in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And if I'm correct from your evidence, you spent most of the time that you were in Herceg-Bosna in Mostar. Is that correct, physically in Mostar? Correct me if I'm wrong, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, did you personally prepare your summary? Did you write it out in your own language and then have it translated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the summary that you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not prepare that summary. On the basis of the interview which Defence counsel had with me, this summary was prepared some seven -- or rather was drafted some seven or eight days before I came to The Hague. And the file version, which I signed, I did that two days before I came to The Hague, which means last Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Sarajevo; in Zagreb, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know English?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some, but I do not think that my knowledge of English -- I'm not proficient enough. I wouldn't dare discuss serious matters in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then you've prepared the summary or you reviewed the summary that was prepared for you in Croatian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help clarify something. I was provided with a copy of the Croatian edition, and in both paragraph 6 and paragraph 50, point 6 and 50, in English, if you have it -- this is the one time I would not object to you taking a look -- but in English, it says in 6: "After the Dayton Agreement in 1996, I became the deputy minister of justice and administration for Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo." And in 50, in English, when you were discussing the conduct of legal analysis, it says: "In my position as deputy minister for the administration of the SR BiH government." I noticed in the Croatian, in 6, point 6, you used one word, and you used a different word in 50, and I think the word that you used in 6 was "zamjnik", and in 50, "pomocnik" or "pomocnik". Do you see a difference? You yourself, in your language, referred to these terms. The translation, however, equates them. Are they absolutely the same?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bearing in mind my knowledge of English, I am really not competent enough to comment on the English translation because I am simply not proficient enough. But in the summary in Croatian, which says that when I came to Sarajevo, I was appointed deputy minister of justice, that is correct. Under the Bosnian-Herzegovinian regulations, there is a significant difference between a deputy minister and an assistant minister. Deputy minister is also a political figure, not merely a professional, and a deputy, like a minister, is subject to rotation after the elections when one loses power, whereas assistant ministers, as professionals, go on with their jobs. So I was a deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You have down "pomocnik", though, for 50, when you're talking about the work in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So you were an assistant minister, is that correct, by your own definition?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assistant minister before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990 and 1991. After the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1995, when I returned to Sarajevo, or rather late 1995 and 1996, that is, I began to work as a deputy minister. That is a higher job, a higher-ranking job, than the assistant minister's job. So that could be the reason for misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It is about the assistant minister job in point 50 you were working that I would like to ask you a few questions. That job does not necessarily commit you to take over the duties of a minister in his absence; is that correct? There is a deputy minister who would take over those functions; am I right? If not, correct me.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 50 relates to the period before the war, when I was an assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And under the regulations and rules in effect in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, the minister of justice -- in the Ministry of Justice, I was responsible for the Department of Administration. That is, the Ministry had several departments, and I was responsible directly for the Department of Administration. If a certain request was filed with the Ministry of Justice dealing with administration, with some administrative matters, then it was the department which I headed. As the chief of that department, it was my task to prepare for the minister of justice the relevant opinion, professional opinion. That opinion, when sent by the ministry to, say, the government, would be sent as the opinion of the ministry. But at the preparatory stage, that is within the jurisdiction of the department which I headed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Getting back to my question: As the assistant minister -- there were a number of them; correct? You were not the only assistant minister; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- before the war, in the Ministry of Justice, there were three assistant ministers. One was responsible for administration and I was the one. A colleague of mine was responsible for judiciary, that is judicial administration. And another colleague was responsible for criminal sanctions, that is, they maintained contact with prisons and were responsible for the enforcement of regulations bearing criminal sanctions. So, the department of administration was responsible for administrative affairs, and I headed it at the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there only one deputy minister to the minister of justice as opposed to the three assistant ministers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a generally-accepted practice that a minister would have just one deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And if the minister were for any reason absent or for any reason unable to fulfil his duties, the deputy minister would take on the job which was really the responsible position next to that of the minister; is that correct? He would run or she would run things.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By statute, by the law in effect then, the administration law in case the minister was absent or prevented from attending, he was being replaced by his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did the deputy or the minister rely completely on assessments of the assistant ministers such as yourself, or were you the last person to render a recommendation or an opinion? Did you take that responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was roughly as follows: The relevant department prepared the regulations which fell within its field of jurisdiction; opinions, decisions and so on and so forth. It would then draft the working draft and then at the meeting of the ministry attended by the minister, deputy and other people, such papers would then be amended, that is, major or smaller changes would be made in such documents. But by and large, not only the case of my department but, generally, the position of the department would, as a rule, be adopted, accepted with possibly minor corrections.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So once -- if corrections were made, you made them and then it went on and that was it; is that correct? The end product was that paper which was produced after corrections and then it went out without change; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It would then go out as the official document of the ministry signed by the minister or the deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you keep a copy of the papers, decisions, documents, recommendations that you made for your own use or perhaps for a future job references or for some other professional need?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All ministries, and they were practically all housed in a big building in central Sarajevo, they all shared the archive and we were bound once a document had been finally written, to file it with the archive. I had some notes or perhaps some briefs in my desk but, unfortunately, I must say that in April 1992, after I left Sarajevo, I already said that I did that around the 20th of April, the archive of our ministry and even our private archive, you may call it that, that is, things that we kept in our desks in our offices, all that stayed behind in the ministry building. The building of the Ministry of Justice and other ministries was under ongoing shelling by the Serbs, for about a year it was under the shelling. A large part of the building burned down and in August 1992, when I returned to Sarajevo, I tried to get to those -- to at least some of those notes because I had left even three professional papers that I was preparing that stayed among other papers. I could not even come close to the building because the then military unit which was standing guard around it because of the -- because the building was exposed to the sniper action, there were only about 100 metres away, not more than that. They simply did not allow me, or anyone else for that matter, to approach the building so that I could not even get -- lay my hands on even my private notes or those professional papers that I was writing, preparing and which, unfortunately, perished.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Before coming to The Hague to give testimony on behalf of Dario Kordic, did you attempt to check with any other archives in Sarajevo or any other part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to find the documents upon which you are basing your statements?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base my testimony on the documentation published in official -- in the Official Gazette and other official organs which were accessible to a huge number of citizens and institutions because they were public. As a man trained in law, I wanted to read the relevant documents, say, about the procedure concerning the appraisal of constitutionality of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and, independently of this case, I was interested in this three years ago when I didn't ever think that I might be -- become a witness. But I was told then that there was a special procedure whereby one had to file a request to see relevant documents from -- in the existing archives and also indicate reasons for which one was seeking access to this documentation. Since my only motive was my lawyer's curiosity to see that, this did not -- this was not accepted as a sufficiently strong reason to allow me such access.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, in fact, just some of the points upon which you have testified certainly are based on documents that would be found in archives. You did not then apply to the archives in -- which have the records of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina inasmuch as you have made statements about the contents of recommendations to that court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that there was a regulation specifying who could seek to see archival documents. So in addition to state institutions and agencies, scientific workers could also apply for that when preparing their papers. Since I could not apply for this documentation through the institution and since I was not preparing any scientific paper, I -- even had I applied for it, I realised I could not, on the grounds of my own curiosity, claim any access to this documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, I guess that it is fortunate that I have a copy of the complete file from the archives so we can discuss the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask please that the registrar distribute two documents. I must apologise to the Court, again, explaining our situation with the content of this witness' summary, we were unable to have full translations but I will ask these things be put on the ELMO consistent with the consideration the Court has given us in this instance and should the Court ask for a complete translation at some later date, I will be very happy to have it provided. But I think at this point for refreshing the witness' recollection, the ELMO procedure will do. I will ask Ms. Verhaag to pass to -- I'm sorry, perhaps the registrar has given an excessive number of copies. There should only be two documents and the one in the centre should have the last words as "Herceg-Bosna" and the other one should have "Bosanka Posavina". They have the same essential headings, they are from the same institution but one of them ends in "Bosanka Posavina" and the other one ends in "Herceg-Bosna". Apologies for any confusion. I'm sorry. Do you have copies? Have you been provided with copies? Mr. Registrar, if you need extra copies, I can provide for the witness; certainly not a problem. If you're short, I can provide another set. THE USHER: Do you have one?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm fine. I have my own. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, when you have a chance to see them -- okay. These documents, Mr. Perkovic, are from the ministry in which you were employed and, in fact, are the judgements, as it were, or recommendations, judgements, that were issued by your ministry to the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. One of them is a decision or a judgement about whether or not to initiate an investigation into the legality or constitutionality of the Croatian Community of the Bosnian Posavina, and the other one is whether or not to initiate an investigation into the constitutionality of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. They are both dated 20th of November, 1991, and were integral parts of the archive of the Constitutional Court, in fact in the folder related to the decision on the constitutionality of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just object to the form of the question. I think that the procedure that must be followed here is to ask him whether these documents do, in fact, come from the ministry by which he was employed because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can be asked whether he can identify the documents. Counsel can't give evidence about where they were found. Some other form of evidence must be called. But the matter can be put before the witness to see whether he identifies the documents. On the whole, Ms. Somers, this procedure should be kept to a minimum, because it's impossible for the Court to follow. Now, let the witness look at the documents to see whether he can identify them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a reservation to make. To my mind, these are not documents of the Ministry of Justice and Administration of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I say that for two reasons. The first one is that under the then regulations, every opinion -- at the end of the document, there should have been the seal and the signature of the authorised person, so the minister, perhaps deputy minister, or if that was an internal act, then the assistant ministers. Secondly, under our legal practice, here we have three completely different bodies. One is the Ministry of Justice and Administration. The second is the Republican -- Establishment for Public Administration, and the third is the professional body of the Bosnian government, which is called the Secretariat for Legislation of the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was not a common practice to have three agencies or two agencies, different institutions, to give one uniform opinion on a text, so I should like to see the official document of the Ministry of Justice and Administration with the seal of the ministry and the signature of the authorised person in that ministry. Because without the signature and the seal, such opinions lacked legal grounds under the then regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. We'll confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, we really must keep this, as I've said, to an absolute minimum. It is obviously fair that you should have the opportunity, where you have such documents, to contradict the witness's evidence, and the course which we shall allow is this: If you say these documents contradict what the witness has said in his evidence, then, in a few words summarising what the document says, you can put it to him so he can have the opportunity to respond and we may know what your case is. Beyond that, we shall not allow you to go. If you wish to call evidence about this matter, then you can do so in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, and again we apologise simply because of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But in order that we keep the proceedings in an orderly fashion, perhaps you would briefly summarise what the documents say and give the witness the opportunity of responding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, if you take a look, please, at the document about Herceg-Bosna, just the very end of it. If you would be kind enough, because I think your Croatian pronunciation is superior to mine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow you to go through the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just the second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would just quickly summarise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, the recommendation as to Herceg-Bosna was that there was a basis for investigating the constitutionality of the decision founding the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and all of the various decisions that were later enumerated, and that is what is enumerated in this document, where it actually says that the -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, in accordance with our regulations, this is not a document, this is no document, this is no official document. It lacks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, we've heard your evidence about that point. What you must answer is this: It's put to you that there is a recommendation in this document that there was a basis for investigating the constitutionality of the decision founding the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now, what the effect of this is, the Prosecution say, so that you can understand it, is that it contradicts your evidence. Is there anything more you would like to say about it, other than comments about the form of the document? We have your evidence about the form of the document. There's no need to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my statement, in response to the question put by the Defence, I said that an opinion went from the Ministry of Justice to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for which I claim with full responsibility that by its very substance it is contrary to what is written here. And I said that on the basis of that opinion, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in November 1992, did not find it necessary to institute proceedings for assessing the constitutionality of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The only thing I can say about this is what I have already said, and I abide by that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Somers, I don't think we're going to take matters very much further.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I just, for completeness, just ask, so that the record reflects what the second document is, in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The second document on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Bosnian Posavina in summary says that your particular ministry did not find a basis for recommending investigation or to open an investigation on the Croatian Community of the Bosnian Posavina, and I distinguish it because it was a political grouping. In other words, it is, as to Posavina, the same position that you said about point 50. That is the point of this document. Is that a fair summary just of the very last parts of the document, that there was a finding of no basis for investigation on constitutionality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I know that the Ministry of Justice, as far as the Croatian Community of Bosanka Posavina is concerned, gave an identical opinion to that provided by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, so it is exactly the same period of time. The opinion was probably sent on the same day or within the scope of two days, and in that context it would have been quite illogical, in the case of one Croat Community, to define one opinion and for another Croat Community to define another, a different opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, in the interests of time, because we must move on, I will just suggest that the bases for the decisions are very different. And if you care to comment, feel free, but that is the essence of why there are different results. When you moved on to Herceg-Bosna, did you ever suggest that some complaint be filed about the decisions by the courts? In other words, if the court in Sarajevo took a decision that you thought was either unjust or without notice, did you do anything about it? Is there a record that you could cite to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina was passed during war conflicts and during the total siege under which Sarajevo was. I said during my testimony that I personally and, I claim, all the other officials that were involved in this subject matter in the institutions of Herceg-Bosna did not know of the proceedings before the Constitutional Court or of this decision having been passed at all until a few months later; after it had been passed, that is. We only had the opportunity of hearing about it. And when it was published in the newspapers that the Constitutional Court had passed such a decision, even if we wanted to, we could not have responded or reacted to such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, the newspapers also, are you aware, just yes or no, that the newspapers also carried a decision about the Posavina result as opposed to the Herceg-Bosna result. Did you read that in Oslobodzenje? Are you familiar with that? That would have been on the 24th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, I lived in Sarajevo and of course I read Oslobodzenje and other newspapers that were printed in Sarajevo. In those newspaper articles at the time, as far as I can remember, it was stated that the constitutionality of these Croat communities of Bosanska Posavina and Herceg-Bosna were inquired about and, of course, the journalists made their own comments about the legality or illegality of these institutions. However, official government institutions until 1993, I think until September of 1993, did not take into consideration or rather did not pass any decisions with regard to the constitutionality of these communities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher, please, to distribute four items. They have been previously marked Z199.1, Z199.2, Z171.1 and then, unfortunately, falling into, I hope, one of the last of the category of untranslateds just as a reference point, a letter of the 23rd of July 1992 signed by Dr. Dautbasic. If you can turn, if we can get beyond it to the untranslated document dated 23rd of July 1992, I will simply ask you if the summary of the content is correct according to your reading. This is a letter to the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo and it is signed by the president of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Dr. Ismet Dautbasic. Essentially, it notifies the receiving party of the examination of the constitutionality and it asks for input; is that a fair, a very brief, rough summary?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I am not denying that the president of the Constitutional Court sent this kind of letter to the Croat Democratic Community in Sarajevo. However, the proceedings before this court were instituted against the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna not against the HDZ as a political party.
